title: Smaller than small, greater than great (3.20)
hookLine: the Upanishad calls the self in your heart tinier than an atom and vaster than the sky, in the same breath
carry: the one in your heart is greater than the sky
tomorrow: bhakti, the love the teaching shines for
last: GOD IS ONE, WITH NO SECOND.

lines: SMALLER THAN A GRAIN OF SAND.
cards: Anor aniyan mahato mahiyan. Two pictures that refuse to sit still together. Smaller than a grain of sand, smaller than anything a microscope can show.
And at the same time bigger than the earth, the sky, every star. Try to hold both, and the mind tends to flip between them like a coin. That flip is what today's verse is after.
It sets the two side by side and says: this is what the self is like.

teach.h: SMALLER THAN SMALL, GREATER THAN GREAT.
teach.b: Verse 3.20, in paraphrase: smaller than the small, greater than the great, the self is hidden in the heart of every creature.
Free of craving, free of sorrow, one sees that Lord and his greatness through the grace of the creator.

Those opening words also appear in the Katha Upanishad, in a nearly identical verse. The difference is at the end. In the Katha, the last phrase is usually read as seeing the self through the calm of the senses.
Here, almost the same sounds are read as through the grace of the creator. A tiny shift, and the verse tilts toward a personal God who gives. Why both small and great?

teach.h: ONE PICTURE WOULD BE A CAGE.
teach.b: Because any single picture would be a cage. Call it small, and you put it in a box. Call it great, and you make it far away.
Say both, and the mind has to let go. Here's the teaching, and it's one of Hinduism's deepest: the God who rules past the stars and the self hidden in your own heart are not two strangers.
It's why a Hindu grandmother can say God is everywhere and, in the same breath, tap your chest.

teach.h: IN THE HEART, BEYOND THE STARS.
teach.b: The seekers asked what the cause is. They saw the wheel, and the swan lost on it, feeling apart. They churned the fire sticks, sat up straight, and named the One.
And today: that One, closer than your heartbeat and bigger than the sky.

how: Many Hindus chant anor aniyan mahato mahiyan as part of Upanishad recitation, and Vedanta teachers often use it to show that the self cannot be pictured by size at all.

o: a slow growth from tiny to vast over time
smaller than the smallest, hidden in the heart
a humble person who makes themselves small

games.q: the week in the Shvetashvatara: tap the pairs.
p: one rim, three tires, fifty spokes
circles until it stops seeing two

s: this verse appears only in the Shvetashvatara
the Katha Upanishad has a nearly identical verse.
the Shvetashvatara's version is read as seeing the self through the grace of the creator
the Katha's is usually read as through the calm of the senses: nearly the same sounds, a different reading.
the verse says the self is hidden in the heart of every creature
smaller than small, greater than great, set in the heart of every being.

games.q: a student asks the teacher: is the self small or great? what does verse 3.20 answer?
o: small: it lives in the heart.
both at once, so that no single picture can hold it.
games.why: smaller than the small, greater than the great. the paradox keeps the mind from boxing the self into any one image.

practice: Rest your attention on a single point at the center of your chest, small as a pinprick, for a few breaths. Then let it widen past your body, the room, the town, out to the sky.
Go back and forth, small then vast, and notice what stays the same while the pictures trade places.

wordCard.voice: Anor aniyan, smaller than the smallest. The first half of the Upanishad's paradox: the self, finer than an atom, hidden in the heart, and also greater than the greatest.

orig.note: Sanskrit aṇor aṇīyān: smaller than the small. paired with mahato mahīyān, greater than the great.

carryVoice: Your line: the one in your heart is greater than the sky. Smaller than small, greater than great. That's week sixty-one.
